synopsis: FMVSS 127 is a US on-road reference for light-vehicle AEB, pedestrian AEB and forward-collision warning up to 4,536 kg GVWR; it does not apply to off-road machines [f2831]. Finalized on 9 May 2024 and amended on 26 November 2024, it identifies 1 September 2029 as the compliance date, but that date is uncertain: DOT announced amendment preparation on 23 March 2026, with a reported two-year extension not established here as enacted [f2832, f2833, f2834, f2877, f10867, f10868]. Requirements include lead-vehicle no-contact avoidance up to 62 mph, pedestrian AEB at 10–73 km/h in daylight and darkness, and detection and communication of sensor-obstruction degradation [f15420, f11691, f2000]. False-activation tests cover a steel trench plate at 80 km/h and passage between parked vehicles, failing when peak deceleration exceeds manual braking by 0.25 g or more; the booklet calls this the clearest published definition of unacceptable unnecessary braking and identifies no off-road equivalent [f15421, f15422, f15438, f15439]. Manufacturers challenged high-speed feasibility and false-activation risk through petitions and a January 2025 lawsuit, while NHTSA called the risk speculative and rejected judging compliance over multiple trials; judicial review has been held in abeyance since February 2025 [f1966, f15425, f1520]. Cost estimates also remain sharply disputed: NHTSA estimates US$354.06 million annually in 2020 dollars versus an industry estimate of US$63 billion reported through a VBOX white paper, whose characterization of both as internally consistent was seen only in a search snippet [f2886, f2888].
